country.comment: Systematic review of empirical studies in developing (low- and middle-income) countries per the 2012 World Bank classification. Across the 28 included studies (9 in South Asia, 8 in Africa, 7 in the Americas and Caribbean, plus studies in Jordan, Azerbaijan, and Turkey/Pakistan/India), 18 countries are studied (Table 2 lists 27 studies across 17 countries, with Zanzibar counted under Tanzania and Trinidad under Trinidad and Tobago; the 28th included study, Cook et al., 2016 [28] in Table 1 and Table 3, is identified in Sections 3.1.3 and 3.3 as rural Kenya, which is also studied in Gulyani et al., 2005 [37]).

effect_estimate.comment: Authors explicitly note that heterogeneity across disciplines, methods, and cost definitions precluded quantitative pooling; numerical ranges and study-specific estimates are synthesized narratively across the 28 cross-sectional studies.
effect_estimate.value: No pooled numeric effect estimate (narrative/thematic synthesis of 28 studies): 15 household coping strategies identified (mean 5 per study), including storage tanks (21/28 studies; 100 to >1,000 L), collecting from alternative sources (17/28; 30 min to 3 h), water treatment (17/28), small-vessel storage (16/28), purchasing water (14/28), drilling wells/boreholes (11/28), and protests/complaints (7/28). Wealthier, more educated, and property-owning households adopt capital-intensive strategies yielding larger supplies (e.g., 200 L/capita/day for well-linked tanks and 150 Lcd for municipal-linked tanks vs. 30 Lcd for alternative-source collection in Delhi, India), whereas low-income and unconnected households bear disproportionate time and financial burdens (collection time = 45% of mean coping costs and 65% among unconnected households in Kathmandu, Nepal, and 56% for poor vs. 34% for wealthier households; total coping costs = 1% to 15% of income, including 15% for low-income vs. 1% for wealthy households in Delhi and median 12% [US$21/month] in rural Kenya, equalling 1x to 6x utility bills even where mandatory fixed charges persist during month-long outages).
effect_estimate.where_found: PDF p. 1, Abstract; PDF pp. 10-14, Sections 3.1-3.5 and Table 3; PDF pp. 16-18, Sections 4 and 5

mechanism_certainty.comment: Capped at <=2 by the systematic review design ceiling (AMSTAR 2), and all 28 included primary studies are cross-sectional. Rated 1 (documented association) because legal/institutional variables—land tenure/property ownership associated with capital-intensive coping (wells/storage tanks), mandatory fixed utility fees/tariffs relative to coping costs and WTP, and unorganised complaints/protests ('voice', noted in 7 studies with little detail and unassessed effectiveness)—are reported via cross-sectional associations and descriptive counts rather than direct empirical observation of administrative mechanisms, while regulatory fragmentation is discussed mainly as policy context in Section 4.
mechanism_certainty.where_found: PDF p. 1, Abstract; PDF p. 4, Section 3; PDF pp. 12-14, Sections 3.1.5, 3.2, 3.3, and 3.5; PDF p. 16, Section 4

mechanism_flags.comment: Examines land tenure and property ownership as determinants of capital-intensive self-supply investments (ELIGIBILITY: tenure, property), mandatory fixed water utility charges during outages, tariff/bill burdens, and coping costs (BURDEN: fees), consumer complaints/protests ('voice') and collective action/community associations pressuring local authorities or funding communal wells (ENFORCEMENT: complaint, participation), and weak/fragmented regulatory oversight of alternative water providers (institutional_fragmentation). Note: 'accommodating' in Section 3.1.2 refers to household behavioural coping (e.g., rescheduling chores), not administrative accommodation.
mechanism_flags.value: ELIGIBILITY, BURDEN, ENFORCEMENT, tenure, property, fees, complaint, participation, institutional_fragmentation
mechanism_flags.where_found: PDF p. 1, Abstract; PDF p. 3, Section 2.1; PDF pp. 11-14, Table 3 and Sections 3.1.5, 3.2, 3.3, and 3.5; PDF pp. 15-16, Section 4

outcome_flags.comment: Review directly synthesizes evidence on household responses to unreliable and intermittent/discontinuous water supply (service_reliability, service_continuity), domestic water access including alternative sources (water_access), water quantities obtained/stored in Lcd (service_quantity), microbial/chemical contamination and household treatment (service_quality), and direct/indirect coping costs relative to household income, utility water bills, and WTP (affordability).
outcome_flags.value: service_reliability, service_continuity, water_access, service_quantity, service_quality, affordability

[28] omitted from Table 2).

study_design.comment: Structured searches across 7 bibliographic databases plus Google, Google Scholar, and reference lists, with quality/risk-of-bias appraisal adapted from Hellebrandt et al. (Cochrane/EPPI domains) and thematic synthesis (no meta-analysis due to methodological and outcome heterogeneity; all 28 included studies used cross-sectional data).
